title: Meena Kumari vs Jyoti Deshmukh on 29 February, 2024
full_text: Meena Kumari vs Jyoti Deshmukh on 29 February, 2024 IN THE COURT OF MS. VINERJEET KAUR MM (N.I. ACT-03) SOUTH-WEST: DWARKA COURTS: NEW DELHI CNR No.DLSW02- 052780-2018 Ct. Case No. 70/19 PS: Palam U/s.138 N.I. Act . MEENA KUMARI VS. JYOTI DESHMUKH Date of Institution of case: 03.01.2019 Date of which Judgment reserved: 15.02.2024 Date on which judgment pronounced: 29.02.2024 JUDGMENT 1) Unique ID no. of the case : DLSW02- 052780-2018 2) Name of complainant : Meena Kumari W/o Sh. Vijay Kumar, R/o B-3, Type-IV, Tower-IV, Kidwai Nagar East, New Delhi-23. 3) Name and address of accused : Jyoti Deshmukh W/o Sh. Rameshwar Deshmukh R/o House No. 4, Pocket B-8, Golf Link, Sector-23B, Dwarka, New Delhi-78. 4) Offence complained of : Section 138 N.I. Act 5) Plea of accused : Accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial 6) Final Order : Acquitted for the offence punishable U/s.138 N.I. Act Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 1/22 7) Date of order : 29.02.2024 BRIEF STATEMENT OF REASONS FOR THE DECISION:- 1. The present complaint has been filed under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter " NI Act ") by Meena Kumari (hereinafter "complainant") against Jyoti Deshmukh (hereinafter "accused"). 2. The substance of allegations, as contained in the complaint, are as follows: A. That on 27.12.2015, the accused approached the complainant for a friendly loan of Rs.5,00,000/- and upon her request, the complainant paid her a sum of Rs.5,00,000/-and the accused assured the complainant that she would return the above said amount within 3 months. That on 19.07.2016, the accused returned the amount of Rs.1,00,000/- through cheque bearing No. 182779 to the complainant. B. Then in the month of November, 2018, the accused issued a cheque bearing No.416321 dated 05.11.2018 of Rs.4,00,000/- drawn on State Bank of India, APRA Plaza II, Plot No.14, Central Market, Sector-10, Dwarka, New Delhi in favour of the complainant. C. On assurance of the accused, the complainant presented the above-mentioned cheque on 05.11.2018 with her banker but the same was returned unpaid by the bankers of the accused with the reasons "Funds Insufficient" vide cheque return memo dated 13.11.2018. D. That thereafter, the complainant sent the accused a legal notice dated 27.11.2018 through her counsel via speed post. Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 2/22 3. Accused's stance, on the contrary, at the stage of framing of notice under section 251 CrPC was that she denied any liability towards the complainant. Further, she stated that she had taken a loan of Rs.1,00,000/- from the complainant which has been repaid to the complainant. The complainant is into committee business and she was the member of that committee (chit fund). She further stated that she had given the cheque in question to the complainant as security for a committee. She further stated that complainant is in the possession of her one more blank signed cheque. She stated that she received the legal notice though she contested this at the stage of final arguments. She admitted her signature on the cheque in question but denied the filling of other particulars there on. 4. Pre-summoning evidence was led by the complainant and on finding a prima facie case, the accused was summoned to face trial. On appearance, the accused was served with the notice of accusation under Section 251 , Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter " CrPC ") to which the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. The accused admitted her signature on the cheque in question but denied filling of other details at this stage. The accused was granted an opportunity to cross-examine the complainant. 5. During the trial, the complainant has led the following oral and documentary evidence against the accused to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt:- Oral Evidence Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 3/22 CW-1/1 Testimony of complainant Documentary Evidence Ex. CW1/A Cheque in question Ex. CW1/B Cheque Return Memo Ex.CW1/C Legal notice Ex.CW1/D Postal receipt 6. Thereafter, before the start of defence evidence, in order to allow the accused to personally explain the circumstances appearing in evidence against her, her statement under Section 313 CrPC was recorded without oath. In reply, the accused submitted the following in her statement under section 313 CrPC: ● The accused admitted that she knew the complainant since past 20 years and they had business relations. The accused further denied that she had approached the complainant on 27.12.2015 for a friendly loan of Rs.5,00,000/-. Rather, in January, 2016, she had taken a loan of Rs.1,00,000/- from the complainant at an interest @ 10% per month to be repaid in six months. At that time, she gave one blank signed cheque of hers as security to the complainant. In order to repay the loan amount, her husband drew one cheque for a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- on his account and the same was honoured. Complainant had told the accused not to fill the name of payee in that cheque. ● She further stated that her husband did not agree on the interest amount which was exorbitant according to him. But she paid the interest amount of Rs.60,000/- in Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 4/22 cash to the complainant. When she asked the complainant to return her security cheque, since, loan amount was already paid to her, she told her to wait till the time, cheque of Rs.1,00,000/- from her husband's account gets honoured. When accused and her husband realized that the cheque of Rs.1,00,000/- was credited in the account of one Ajay then again she approached the complainant to return her security cheque but she told her that she had misplaced the same. The same security cheque was misused by the complainant through one Ajay Dahiya who had filed a complaint case u/s 138 NI Act in which she got acquitted. Complainant used to run a committee of which she was a member and the cheque in question was given as security cheque in blank signed manner to the complainant for the committee. The complainant has misused the same by filing the present complaint case. The accused denied any liability towards the complainant. She received legal demand notice and replied to the same. ● The accused further stated that she received the legal notice sent by the complainant. The accused took the same stance as in her defence while framing notice under Section 251 CrPC. 7. The accused opted to lead defence evidence during the statement under Section 313 CrPC, and he examined four witness, she examined himself as DW-1, DW-2 Sh. Amitendu Rawat, DW-3 ASI Jyoti Swarup and DW-4 Sh. Ajay Kumar. 8. Thereafter, the matter was listed for final arguments. After listening to final arguments from both sides, the matter was reserved for pronouncement. I have heard Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 5/22 the learned counsels on both the sides and have given my thoughtful consideration to the material appearing on record. 9. Before appreciation of evidence led on behalf of the parties, I would like to narrate the legal principles, relevant for adjudication of complaint under Section 138 of NI Act. 10. Section 138 of Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 makes dishonour of cheques an offence. It provides that: "where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both". 11. In order to ascertain whether the accused has committed an offence u/s 138 NI Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 6/22 Act, the following ingredients constituting the offence have to be proved: (i) The drawer of the cheque should have issued the cheque for the discharge, in whole or in part of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. (ii) The cheque is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that bank. (iii) The drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money within fifteen days of the receipt of the notice from the payee or the holder in due course demanding the payment of the said amount of money. It is only when all the above-mentioned ingredients are satisfied that the person who has drawn the cheque can be said to have committed an offence u/s 138 NI Act. 12. It is important to reproduce Sec.118 and Sec.139 of the NI Act here. Section 118 (a) of the NI Act provides that: "until the contrary is proved, it shall be presumed that "that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration." Further, Section 139 of the NI Act lays down that: "it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 7/22 of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability. 13. The combined effect of section 118(a) NI Act and section 139 of the NI Act is that a presumption exists that the cheque was drawn for consideration and given by the accused for the discharge of debt or other liability. In Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee (2001) 6 SCC 16), their Lordships of Hon'ble Supreme Court observed as follows: Because both Sections 138 and 139 require that the Court "shall presume" the liability of the drawer of the cheques for the amounts for which the cheques are drawn, as noted in State of Madras vs. A. Vaidyanatha Iyer AIR 1958 SC 61, it is obligatory on the Court to raise this presumption in every case where the factual basis for the raising of the presumption had been established. "It introduces an exception to the general rule as to the burden of proof in criminal cases and shifts the onus on to the accused" (ibid). Such a presumption is a presumption of law, as distinguished from a presumption of fact which describes provisions by which the court "may presume" a certain state of affairs. Presumptions are rules of evidence and do not conflict with the presumption of innocence, because by the latter all that is meant is that the prosecution is Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 8/22 obliged to prove the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt. In this regard, the Hon'ble Apex Court, having analysed all the concerned provisions in Basalingappa Vs. Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418 : 2019 SCC OnLine SC 491 at page 432, came down to the following conclusion: "25. We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Section 118(a) and 139 , we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in the following manner: 25.1. Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of theAct mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability. 25.2. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise probable defence. The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities. 25.3. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence. Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely. Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 9/22 25.4. That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence. Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden. 25.5. It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence." 14. In this case, issuance of cheque, its presentation and dishonouring are not in dispute, inasmuch as the same have been duly proved on the basis of cogent evidence as well as admitted by the accused. The signature on the cheque in question Ex.CW1/A is admitted by the accused. The aforesaid cheque in question was returned unpaid vide return memo bearing Ex.CW1/B. The legal notice bearing Ex.CW1/C was sent to the accused vide postal receipt bearing Ex.CW1/D. In this regard, plea of defence of the accused in notice of accusation framed against her under section 251 CrPC as well as in her statement recorded under Section 313 Cr.PC, the accused admitted that the cheque in question was signed by her. As far as the receipt of legal demand notice is concerned, I shall discuss the same at a later stage of this judgments. 15. In view of the above-mentioned circumstances, the presumptions under sections 139 and 118 NI Act that the cheque in question was for a legally recoverable debt/liability stand activated. 16. Simply stated, the accused has to offer on something that makes his version Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 10/22 probable. This the accused can do by both successfully raising and proving competing version to the case of the complainant or by perforating the case of the complainant. Opportunity to do this arises for the accused at four stages: - (i) When the accused puts forth defence at the time when his plea of defence as recorded after the substance of acquisition explained to him u/s 251 CrPC (ii) When the accused cross examines the complainant pursuant to his application u/S.145(2) N.I. Act being allowed. (iii) When statement of the accused is recorded u/s 313 CrPC and (iv) When defence witness was examined. 17. The stand taken by the accused at all these stages shall be examined to determine if the accused could raise a probable defence. It is evident that the onus was on the accused to rebut the statutory presumption. Therefore, the accused was required to bring on record such facts and circumstances, which would make the court believe that she had not issued the cheque in question for the alleged purpose and that the complainant had misused her cheque. 18. The argument raised by the accused is that in March 2017, the complainant had approached her for starting one committee of Rs.2,00,000/- consisting of 10 members each paying a share of Rs.20,000/- per month. In April 2017, her name was declared in the second committee and she received a sum of Rs.1,80,000/-. The complainant took the cheque in question as security at the time of releasing the said amount. Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 11/22 Thereafter, in June 2017, she came to know that another cheque which she had given to the complainant on an earlier date and which she had allegedly misplaced was presented in the bank and dishonoured. When she confronted the complainant about the same, the complainant turned a deaf ear. The accused stated that she had filed a complaint before the SHO Dwarka regarding that cheque against the complainant and two others and this complaint was filed in response to the complaint filed by her. She further stated that she had borrowed a sum of Rs 1,00,000/- from the complainant in 2016, but had already repaid that along with interest of Rs 60,000/- and therefore did not owe any money to the complainant. Her defence is that the complainant has misused the cheque in question with a malicious intention. She has raised various points to show that the complaint is not maintainable and further that she does not owe any legal liability to the complainant. 19. The first objection raised on behalf of the accused is that the offence under section 138 NI Act, 1881 is not made out as the legal notice dated 23.12.2019 was not served upon her. In fact, no tracking report has been filed by the complainant. She further states that even the address mentioned on the legal notice is not her correct address. The accused had admitted receiving the legal notice at the stage of framing of notice against her but had later explained that she answered yes as she got confused . In fact the address she gave at that stage was different in the sense that the flat number was 484 and in the address on the legal notice it was 489. Thereafter the burden to prove that the address mentioned on the legal notice was the correct address Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 12/22 of the accused was on the complainant. However, the complainant could not prove that the address on the legal notice was that of the accused. It is not even the case that the summons were served on the same address. They were returned with the report that no such person resides on this address. The court at the stage of the final arguments under Section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act asked the accused to produce her Aadhar card and took a copy of the same on record. According to the address mentioned on her Aadhar card, her flat number was indeed 484 and not 489. To constitute an offence under Section 138 NI Act, sending or giving of legal demand notice is not enough, it is the 'receipt of notice' by the drawer or his agent that is critical. In K. Bhaskaran v. Sankaran Vaidhyan Balan & Anr , The Supreme Court held that, the failure on the part of the drawer to pay the amount should be within 15 days 'of the receipt of the said notice. It is, therefore, clear that 'giving notice' in the context is not akin to 'receipt of notice'. It is duty of payee to send the notice to the correct address. In D. Vinod Shivappa v. Nanda Belliappa , the question before the Court was whether in a case where the postal endorsement showed that the notice could not be served on account of the non availability of the addressee, a cause of action could still arise for prosecution of the drawer of the cheque on the basis of deemed service of notice under clause (c) of proviso to Section 138 NI Act. The Court held that, this question had to be answered by reference to the facts of each case and no rule of universal application could be laid down that in all cases where notice was not served on account of non-availability of the addressee, the Court must presume service of notice. It elaborated as follows, "If a notice is issued and served upon the Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 13/22 drawer of the cheque, no controversy arises. Similarly if the notice is refused by the addressee, it may be presumed to have been served. This is also not disputed. This leaves us with the third situation where the notice could not be served on the addressee for one or the other reason, such as his non availability at the time of delivery, or premises remaining locked on account of his having gone elsewhere etc. If in each such case the law is understood to mean that there has been no service of notice, it would completely defeat the very purpose of the Act. It would then be very easy for an unscrupulous and dishonest drawer of a cheque to make himself scarce for sometime after issuing the cheque so that the requisite statutory notice can never be served upon him and consequently he can never be prosecuted. There is good authority to support the proposition that once the complainant, the payee of the cheque, issues notice to the drawer of the cheque, the cause of action to file a complaint arises on the expiry of the period prescribed for payment by the drawer of the cheque. If the complainant is able to prove that the drawer of the cheque knew about the notice and deliberately evaded service and got a false endorsement made only to defeat the process of law, the Court shall presume service of notice. This, however, is a matter of evidence and proof. Thus even in a case where the notice is returned with the endorsement that the premises has always been found locked or the addressee was not available at the time of postal delivery, it will be open to the complainant to prove at the trial by evidence that the endorsement is not correct and that the addressee, namely the drawer of the cheque, with knowledge of the notice had deliberately avoided to receive notice. The question as to whether the service of notice Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 14/22 has been fraudulently refused by unscrupulous means is a question of fact to be decided on the basis of evidence". The Apex Court reiterated in Dalmia Cement (Bharat) Ltd. v. M/s Galaxy Traders that, it is not the 'giving' of the notice which makes the offence but it is the 'receipt' of the notice and non payment thereafter, by the drawer which gives the cause of action to the complainant to file the complaint within the statutory period. The Hon'ble HC of Delhi in RL Varma and Sons (HUF) v PC Sharma, CRL. REV. P. 438/2017 held that when notice is sent at the wrong address, the presumption of service under section 27 of GCA r/w section 114 of Indian Evidence Act (hereinafter IEA) do not apply. It was held that, Legal presumption of service of notice can only arise in case the notice is correctly addressed. If the notice is incorrectly addressed no legal presumption can arise. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act mandates the issuance of the statutory notice as a pre-condition to filing of a complaint. The cause of action to file a complaint under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act arises only on issuance and service of statutory notice and failure of the accused to comply with the statutory notice. In the absence of service of statutory notice the cause of action would not accrue. Service of statutory notice would also include legal presumption of service if circumstances so warrant. As the legal notice was incorrectly addressed and consequently, there was no service on the accused, the legal notice will not be deemed to have been served and therefore the offence under section 138 of negotiable instruments act is not made out. 20. The next defence raised by the accused is that though the complainant during Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 15/22 her cross examination on 22.03.2022 stated that she had given the money to the accused in front of her husband and her children and further on 21.12. 2022 stated that her husband and children were also present at the time of receiving the cheque from the accused, she has not examined them. The accused has argued that the complainant could have examined the witnesses if she had come to the court with clean hands and they had indeed witnessed the transactions as alleged by the complainant, after she was questioned about it during her cross examination. Further, the complainant during the cross examination has stated that she borrowed the money she gave to the accused from her husband and her brother-in-law. However, she did not examine them about the same. They accused as argued that the failure on the part of the complainant to examine the major witnesses shows that she has not come to the court with clean hands and has filed a false case against her. 21. The next argument raised by the accused is that the complainant did not have the financial capacity to give her the loan amount of Rs.5,00,000/- as alleged by her. She has examined the chief manager of Indian bank who had brought the statement of account of the complainant for the period from 1 December 2015 till 1 January 2016, and the same was exhibit as DW2/A. As per the statement, there was no major withdrawal of money during this period and the balance amount in the account of the complainant was Rs.3290/- only. They accused has argued that it is unlikely that a person who would have only Rs.3290/- in her account would give a loan of Rs.5,00,000/- to another person. Further, she has not examined her husband or brother- Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 16/22 in-law to prove that they had lent her the money. In fact, when asked to produce the bank statement, the complainant failed to do so. The accused has also argued that it is unlikely that a person who gives a loan of Rupees Five Lakh would not execute any document while advancing this amount. She had not got any receipt or acknowledgement signed by the accused. Further, she cannot produce any correspondence between the parties in the form of Whatsapp or text messages wherein she had demanded the money from the accused. All these factors go on to show that the complainant could not have and did not advance the sum of Rs.5,00,000/-to the accused as alleged by her. 22. The accused has also argued that the complainant has not been consistent in her testimony. She has stated different things at different stages and that is enough to rebut the presumption raised against the accused. Firstly, the complainant in her evidence affidavit and complaint has stated that she advance the money to the accused on 27 December 2015. However, during her cross examination on 21.12.2022, she said that, 'I had paid Rs.5,00,000/- to the accused in two installments of Rs.2,50,000/- each. First installment of Rs.2,50,000 was given on 27 December 2015, and the balance amount of Rs.2,50,000 was given after two months to the accused.' Secondly, in her complaint, the complainant stated that in the month of November 2018, the accused issued the cheque in question for a sum of Rs.4,00,000/-, but during her cross examination on 21.12.2022, she stated that she does not remember as to whether the cheque was handed over when the first installment was paid or at the time of giving Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 17/22 the second installment. Further again on 07.02,2023 she stated that the said cheque was handed over to her when she advanced the loan amount of Rs.5,00,000/- on 27.12.2015. Thirdly, the complainant, during the cross examination stated that there were no transactions between her brother in law Ajay and the husband of the accused. However, during the defence evidence, Mr Ajay Kumar was summoned along with his bank statement which was exhibit as DW4/A. As per the bank statement, a sum of Rs.1,00,000/- was deposited into the account of Mr Ajay vide a cheque on 19 July 2016 from the account of the husband of the accused. The accused stated that this one lakh is the amount that she had borrowed from the complainant and had subsequently repaid through a cheque issued from her husbands account. This statement of the accused was not challenged by the complainant. The above mentioned contradictions show that the complainant has constantly changed her statements. The accused has argued that this would not have been the case if the complainant was telling the truth. She has been improving her statements to fit whatever narrative she deems best at different stages, thereby betraying her dishonesty. This conduct of the complainant raises serious doubts about the credibility of her claims. 23. Accused has further argued that the version presented by her has been coroborated at various places with the help of evidence. She has relied upon cheque number 416314 drawn on State Bank of India on 21.04.2016 for a sum of Rs.60,000/- which has been exhibited as Ex.CW1/DX1. The cheque was produced by the complainant after being asked to do so during her cross examination. As per the Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 18/22 accused this cheque is evendence of a fact that the complainant had charged her and interest @10% per month or an amount of Rs.1,00,000/-. She has argued that the complainant has no reasonable explanation as to why she has the said cheque in her possession. Further, the accused has relied upon the complaint filed by her in the court of Ld. CMM against the complainant and others which is exhibited as Ex.DW1/B. The complaint is dated 07.07.2018 which is before the date of the presentation of the cheque. The accused has asserted that the present complaint was filed in order to get back at her for filing the abovementioned complaint before the Ld. CMM. The complainant has failed to respond to this argument, hence, the court is inclined to believe that she had a motive to file the present complaint. Thereafter, the accused has also relied upon a Judgment of the Court of Judicial Magistrate First Class, Panepat which is Ex.DW1/A. The said judgment has acquitted the accused in a complaint filed by one Ajay Dahiya who the accused asserts is an aquaintance of the complainant and in connivance with whom the present complaint has been filed. The complainant has failed to respond to this argument also.The version presented by the accused has been supported by reliable evidence at different stages and at the same time the accused has successfully pointed out the loop holes in the case of the complainant. All this is sufficient to rebut the presumption that has been raised against the accused. 24. The stand taken by the accused at various stages has be examined to determine if the accused could raise a probable defence on the touchstone of benchmark set in the judgment as held by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Kumar Exports vs Sharma Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 19/22 Carpets (2009)2 SCC 513, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court had held as follows: "The accused in a trial under Section 138 of the Act has two options. He can either show that consideration and debt did not exist or that under the particular circumstances of the case the nonexistence of consideration and debt is so probable that a prudent man ought to suppose that no consideration and debt existed. To rebut the statutory presumptions an accused is not expected to prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt as is expected of the complainant in a criminal trial. The accused may adduce direct evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration and that there was no debt or liability to be discharged by him. However, the court need not insist in every case that the accused should disprove the nonexistence of consideration and debt by leading direct evidence because the existence of negative evidence is neither possible nor contemplated. At the same time, it is clear that bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt, apparently would not served the purpose of the accused. Something which is probable has to be brought on record for getting the burden of proof shifted to the complainant. To disprove the presumptions, the accused should bring on record such facts and circumstances, upon consideration of which, the court may either believe that the consideration and debt did not exist or their nonexistence was so probable that a prudent man would under the circumstances of the case, act upon the plea that they did not exist. Apart from adducing direct Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 20/22 evidence to prove that the note in question was not supported by consideration or that he had not incurred any debt or liability, the accused may also rely upon circumstantial evidence and if the circumstances so relied upon are compelling, the burden may likewise shift again on to the complainant. The accused may also rely upon presumptions of fact, for instance, those mentioned in Section 114 of the Evidence Act to rebut the presumptions arising under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act. The accused has also an option to prove the nonexistence of consideration and debt or liability either by letting in evidence or in some clear and exceptional cases, from the case set out by the complainant, that is, the averments in the complaint, the case set out in the statutory notice and evidence adduced by the complainant during the trial. Once such rebuttal evidence is adduced and accepted by the court, having regard to all the circumstances of the case and the preponderance of probabilities, the evidential burden shifts back to the complainant and, thereafter, the presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the Act will not again come to the complainant's rescue." 25. The accused was required to bring on record such facts and circumstances, which would make the court believe that she did not owe any legal liability to the complainant and that the complainant has misused the cheque. Considering the discussion above, it seems reasonable to say that the accused has been able to establish Ct. Case No.70/2019 Meena Kumari Vs. Jyoti Deshmukh 21/22 her version of events. Therefore, the court is of the view that the cheque is question was not issued for discharge of legally enforceable debt of Rs. 4 Lakh. The complainant has misused the cheque. The accused has still been able to raise a probable defence. Since the accused has discharged the burden it was the complainant who has to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt but has failed to do so. 26. To recapitulate the above discussion, the complainant has been unsuccessful in establishing her case beyond reasonable doubt that the accused had issued the cheque in question in discharge of her legally enforceable liability. The presumptions under Section 118 and Section 139 of N.I. Act have been successfully rebutted. The accused has been able to raise a probable defence. The defence of the accused that the complainant misused the cheque in question and there was no legal liability of Rupees Four Lakh is proved on the standard of preponderance of probabilities. 27. Resultantly, the complaint of the complainant is dismissed, and the accused Jyoti Deshmukh, is hereby acquitted of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.
